evidence.claim: Before the driving route, the Teche served as the principal transportation corridor for the eighteenth-century Acadian migration into this region.
evidence.quote: During the 18th-century Acadian migration to the area - then known as the Attakapas region - the Teche was the primary means of transportation.

evidence.claim: Crossings helped settlements grow: at Breaux Bridge, an 1817 wagon bridge replaced the earlier footbridge and supported commerce.

evidence.claim: At Shadows-on-the-Teche, that economy depended on enslaved people.

evidence.claim: Logging drew workers into the Atchafalaya Basin, where cypress supplied lumber for houses and businesses.
evidence.quote: Others became loggers and harvested the plentiful Cypress trees in the Atchafalaya Basin. These trees were used to build towns, houses and businesses.

evidence.claim: Oil and gas later brought offshore work.
evidence.quote: As time passed, occupations and trade of the settlers changed. Oil and gas were introduced and offshore oil rigs became places of work.

evidence.claim: The town’s name began as a direction to a crossing.
evidence.quote: When traveling directions were given, residents would often instruct people to "go to Breaux's bridge . . ."  This was later adopted as the city's name.

evidence.claim: Firmin Breaux built a footbridge over the Teche in 1799 for family and neighbors.
evidence.quote: In 1799, Breaux built a footbridge across the Bayou Têche to help his family and neighbors make the passage.

evidence.claim: It was a suspension bridge, tied to pilings and large live oaks on both banks.
evidence.quote: It was stabilized by being tied to small pilings located at each end of the bridge as well as to a pair of huge live oak trees on both sides of the bayou.

evidence.claim: It was a suspension bridge, tied to pilings and large live oaks on both banks.

evidence.claim: Chitimacha women continue weaving rivercane baskets, typically using yellow, red and black.
evidence.quote: Among their arts, Chitimacha women weave highly refined baskets from rivercane. They typically use three colors: yellow, red, and black.

evidence.claim: Women also called for help when unpaid taxes threatened the tribe’s remaining land.
evidence.quote: sometimes members were forced to sell land because they could not afford taxes.
